provinces.name: Alberta
provinces.analysis:
Alberta's unemployment rate registered 6.3% in February 2026, down from 6.4% the prior month, with the employment rate at 64.4% and the participation rate at 68.7%; CPI inflation moderated to +3.4% year-over-year from +4.9% previously.1 Provincial housing starts reached 48,438 units in February 2026, compared with 48,896 in the prior period.2

Alberta's energy sector operated against WTI crude at $102.18/bbl and AECO natural gas at $2.846/GJ during the reference week, with energy exports — crude oil, natural gas, and petrochemicals — to the United States representing approximately 90% of provincial crude oil trade.12 Provincial GDP expanded +2.7% in 2024, reflecting conditions across energy and non-energy sectors.13

Alberta Budget 2026, presented by Finance Minister Nate Horner, projects deficits of $4.1 billion for fiscal year 2025-26, $9.4 billion for 2026-27, and $7.6 billion for 2027-28, with the government indicating continued investment in infrastructure and workforce development.3,4 The budget includes an increase to the Tourism Levy from 4% to 6% effective April 1, 2026, while income taxes remain frozen; the Calgary Chamber of Commerce described the 2026-2029 period as one of protracted deficits.5,7

The federal government committed $730,538 through the Rural Transit Solutions Fund to support transit purchase and planning projects across six rural Alberta communities.8,9 In Calgary, the public hearing on Bylaw 9P2026 — which would repeal Blanket Rezoning amendments implementing citywide residential rezoning under Land Use Bylaw 1P2007 — recessed on March 23 and is scheduled to resume April 2, 2026.10
provinces.sectorHighlights:
Alberta's oil and gas sector — the province's dominant export industry — operates with WTI crude at $102.18/bbl and AECO natural gas at $2.846/GJ; the United States absorbs approximately 90% of Alberta's crude oil exports.12 National Mining and Oil & Gas industry GDP data is not available for the current reference period; energy royalty revenues remain a primary component of Alberta's fiscal base as Budget 2026 projects $9.4 billion in deficit spending for 2026-27 notwithstanding current commodity price levels.4

Alberta's government and public administration sector reflects the fiscal commitments in Budget 2026, with the province projecting deficits across a three-year horizon while signalling infrastructure and workforce development investments.3,6 A federal transfer of $730,538 through the Rural Transit Solutions Fund supports six rural Alberta communities in transit purchase and planning, representing activity at the intersection of federal infrastructure programming and provincial rural transport needs.8,9

Calgary's residential sector faces a regulatory decision point as the public hearing on Bylaw 9P2026 — citywide residential rezoning — is scheduled to resume April 2, 2026, with the outcome determining the scope of as-of-right residential development permitted across the city's land base.10
provinces.labourDeepDive:
Alberta's participation rate declined to 68.7% in February 2026 from 69.0% the prior month, while the employment rate edged down from 64.5% to 64.4% over the same period.1 The unemployment rate fell from 6.4% to 6.3%; the simultaneous decline in both the participation rate and unemployment rate indicates that some individuals exited the labour force during the reference period rather than transitioning into employment.1

Provincial housing starts of 48,438 units in February 2026 — down from 48,896 the prior period — provide a partial indicator of labour demand in construction trades.2 Budget 2026 references investment in workforce development without specifying employment projections; no sector-specific hiring spike or layoff data appeared in available articles for the reference week.6
provinces.consumerPulse:
The Alberta Tourism Levy increases from 4% to 6% effective April 1, 2026 under Budget 2026, raising costs for hotel accommodation and short-term rentals across the province.5 CPI inflation in Alberta registered +3.4% year-over-year in February 2026, down from +4.9% the prior period, indicating a deceleration in the rate of price increase at the provincial level.1

In Calgary, the public hearing on the repeal of citywide Blanket Rezoning (Bylaw 9P2026) continues to April 2, 2026, with the regulatory outcome bearing directly on residential supply conditions and housing availability across the city.10
provinces.tradeExposure: WTI crude oil traded at $102.18/bbl during the reference week, with AECO natural gas at $2.846/GJ; the United States is the destination for approximately 90% of Alberta's crude oil exports, exposing provincial royalty revenues to US demand conditions and cross-border energy price differentials.12 Alberta Budget 2026 projects multi-year deficits totalling over $20 billion across the 2025-28 fiscal period, reflecting the province's sustained spending commitments relative to resource revenue inflows at current commodity price levels.4,5
provinces.marketContext: The Bank of Canada's policy rate stands at 2.25%, setting the benchmark cost of borrowing for capital projects, mortgage financing, and provincial debt issuance in Alberta.11 Alberta Budget 2026 projects deficit financing of $9.4 billion in 2026-27, meaning the province will access bond markets at rates benchmarked against the BoC overnight rate and Government of Canada yields; the cost of that financing directly affects the total fiscal burden of the multi-year deficit projections.4

Finance Minister Brenda Bailey tabled BC Budget 2026 on February 17, 2026, allocating $400 million for BC's new long-term economic strategy alongside investments in skills training, health care, child care, and K-12 education.3 The budget makes expenditure constraint choices the province describes as protecting fiscal stability while advancing the energy transition and boosting competitiveness.4

provinces.name: Saskatchewan
provinces.analysis:
Saskatchewan's unemployment rate rose to 5.6% in February 2026 from 5.3% the prior month, while the employment rate declined to 63.4% from 64.0% and the participation rate fell to 67.1% from 67.6%.1 Provincial CPI registered at -0.7% year-over-year in February 2026, compared to +1.2% in the prior period, and annual GDP growth stood at +3.4% for 2024.1

The 2026-27 provincial budget, tabled on March 18, 2026, projects an $819 million deficit, with the province not projecting a return to surplus until the end of the decade.4 The budget includes tax cuts estimated to generate approximately $200 million in total savings, raises the large financial institution capital tax rate to six percent from four percent, and eliminates the 0.7 percent capital tax on small institutions.5 Scotiabank Economics described the budget as projecting a higher deficit that gradually returns to balance over a five-year plan.6

The federal and Saskatchewan governments announced a joint program to support workers affected by tariffs and global market shifts, with Secretary of State Buckley Belanger and Minister Eric Schmalz appearing in Prince Albert for the announcement.3 The initiative targets workers in industries and communities facing trade-related disruptions across the province.3

The Government of Saskatchewan committed $2 million in 2026-27 to expand its Electronic Monitoring Program by 100 additional GPS-enabled units.8 The province also extended its out-of-province breast cancer diagnostics initiative for an additional year to maintain patient access while managing local wait times and capacity.9

Housing starts in Saskatchewan totalled 5,486 units in February 2026, an increase from 5,327 in the prior period, according to CMHC data.2 CN Rail conducted overnight track repairs at the 51st Street crossing in Saskatoon between Warman Road and Millar Avenue, requiring a temporary road closure beginning March 29, 2026.10
provinces.sectorHighlights:
Saskatchewan's commodity-exposed sectors are tracked against WTI crude at $102.18 per barrel and spring wheat at $607.25 this week, with resource revenues a central variable in the province's 2026-27 budget projections.6 The province's potash export sector drives more than $7 billion in annual export revenues, with global fertilizer demand setting benchmark pricing for provincial producers.7 The federal-provincial tariff worker support program announced in Prince Albert targets workers across resource and agricultural industries facing trade-related disruptions.3

The healthcare sector recorded two program developments this week: the extension of the out-of-province breast cancer diagnostics initiative for an additional year and the launch of the Health Careers 20L high school course providing students with early exposure to healthcare careers.912 National healthcare GDP data was not reported for the current period.

Saskatchewan's residential construction sector recorded 5,486 housing starts in February 2026, up from 5,327 in the prior period, according to CMHC data.2 National construction GDP data was not reported for the current period, limiting direct sector comparison.
provinces.labourDeepDive:
Saskatchewan's participation rate declined to 67.1% in February 2026 from 67.6% in the prior period, and the employment rate fell to 63.4% from 64.0%, alongside an increase in the unemployment rate from 5.3% to 5.6%.1 The simultaneous decline in both the participation rate and employment rate indicates movement out of the labour force as well as into unemployment during the reference period.1

The federal-provincial tariff worker support program announced in Prince Albert this week identifies trade-related employment disruption as a factor affecting specific industries and communities in Saskatchewan.3 The 2026 Skills Canada Saskatchewan Provincial Competition brought nearly 300 high school students, post-secondary students, and apprentices to Regina to demonstrate vocational and technical skills across multiple trades and technology disciplines.13
provinces.consumerPulse: The 2026-27 provincial budget includes tax cuts generating approximately $200 million in total savings for residents and businesses, with increases to child tax benefits among the measures announced.514 Saskatchewan's provincial CPI registered at -0.7% year-over-year in February 2026, compared to +1.2% in the prior period, indicating a broadly lower consumer price environment relative to the same period the prior year.1 The budget projects an $819 million deficit amid trade uncertainty, with the province not returning to surplus until the end of the decade.4
provinces.tradeExposure:
WTI crude oil traded at $102.18 per barrel this week, above typical breakeven thresholds for Saskatchewan's conventional oil producers, contributing to the resource revenue base reflected in provincial budget projections.6 Spring wheat prices stood at $607.25 per bushel, relevant to Saskatchewan's position as a major producer of hard red spring wheat and canola for export markets.7

Potash exports drive more than $7 billion annually in Saskatchewan export revenues, with global fertilizer demand setting benchmark pricing for provincial producers.7 The federal-provincial tariff worker support program signals that shifting trade conditions are identified as affecting Saskatchewan's export-oriented industries, including agriculture and resources.3
provinces.marketContext: The Bank of Canada's policy rate held at 2.25% as of March 31, 2026, setting borrowing cost context for capital projects across Saskatchewan's resource, residential, and infrastructure sectors.11 The 2026-27 provincial budget projects an $819 million deficit while capital allocations for programs such as the Electronic Monitoring expansion take effect in the new fiscal year beginning April 1, 2026.4

provinces.name: Manitoba
provinces.analysis:
Manitoba's unemployment rate fell to 5.7% in February 2026, from 6.3% the prior period, according to Statistics Canada data.1 The provincial employment rate registered 62.5% against a prior reading of 62.9%, and the participation rate declined to 66.3% from 67.1%.1 Provincial GDP grew +1.1% in 2024 on an annual basis.1

Manitoba released Budget 2026 on March 24, 2026, projecting total provincial spending of $27.3 billion — an increase of $1.4 billion, or approximately 5.4%, from 2025-26.2 The budget removes the provincial sales tax from all food sold in grocery stores effective July 1, 2026, and presents a path toward balancing the province's fiscal position.3 A Scotiabank fiscal analysis notes the deficit reduction trajectory is largely unchanged from the prior outlook and is contingent on federal transfers being realized as projected.4

A food industry advocacy group stated the Manitoba budget does not extend the PST exemption to restaurant meals, leaving that food services segment outside the fiscal measure.11 The Canadian Centre for Innovation published a brief recommending Manitoba maintain its sovereign, value-added economic strategy in Budget 2026, with reference to provincial investment in higher-value manufacturing and technology sectors.8

Manitoba's agriculture sector is linked to spring wheat, which traded at $607.25 this week, with canola and nickel from the Thompson mining region constituting additional key export commodities.5 CentrePort Canada, the province's tri-modal inland port in Winnipeg, connects Manitoba's commodity exports to US midwest rail and highway corridors.5

The City of Winnipeg set March 23, 2026 as the final deadline for a $23 million settlement payment from the Caspian defendants related to the Winnipeg Police Service headquarters project, with the city prepared to seek a court judgment for the full $28 million if unpaid.6 The city separately awarded a new contract to Main Street Project for 24/7 mobile outreach services, continuing a homelessness support program funded by the city since April 2021.7
provinces.sectorHighlights:
Manitoba's government and fiscal sector was the week's most active, with Budget 2026 released on March 24, 2026 setting provincial spending at $27.3 billion for 2026-27, up $1.4 billion from 2025-26.23 National industry GDP data were not available for this reporting period, limiting cross-sector contextualization. The budget's PST removal on grocery store food and the overall spending increase are the dominant fiscal signals for Manitoba this week.

Manitoba's municipal infrastructure sector recorded two operational developments: the North End Wastewater Treatment Plant (NEWPCC) restored UV treatment operations on March 18, 2026, resuming normal waterway access for Red River users;9 and the City of Winnipeg completed a scheduled IT network upgrade overnight on March 26-27, 2026, aimed at improving municipal system security and reliability.13 The Winnipeg Police Service headquarters litigation deadline passed on March 23, with the city positioned to pursue the full $28 million court judgment if the $23 million settlement was not received.6
provinces.labourDeepDive:
Manitoba's participation rate fell 80 basis points to 66.3% in February 2026 from 67.1% the prior period, while the employment rate declined 40 basis points to 62.5% from 62.9%, according to Statistics Canada.1 The unemployment rate simultaneously improved 60 basis points to 5.7%, a combination indicating that some of the unemployment decline coincides with labour force exits rather than employment gains alone.1

No sector-specific hiring data, layoff reports, wage trends, or youth and immigration labour dynamics were present in this week's Manitoba news coverage. Manitoba CMHC-tracked housing starts registered 7,642 annualized units in February 2026, down from 7,799 in the prior period, indicating a modest pullback in residential construction activity.10
provinces.consumerPulse: Manitoba's Budget 2026 removes the provincial sales tax from all food sold in grocery stores starting July 1, 2026, representing the main consumer-facing fiscal measure in this week's provincial announcements.3 A food industry advocacy group stated the exemption does not cover restaurant meals, leaving that segment subject to existing PST rates.11 No additional consumer price, energy cost, or retail trend data were present in this week's Manitoba news coverage.
provinces.tradeExposure: Spring wheat traded at $607.25 this week, serving as the primary commodity benchmark for Manitoba's agriculture-dependent export economy alongside canola.5 Nickel from the Thompson mining region adds a metals export dimension to Manitoba's commodity profile. CentrePort Canada, Canada's only tri-modal inland port located in Winnipeg, routes Manitoba goods to US midwest markets via road, rail, and air, providing a key logistics node for agricultural and manufactured exports.5
provinces.marketContext: The Bank of Canada held its policy rate at 2.25% as of March 31, 2026, setting the baseline capital cost environment for Manitoba's projected $27.3 billion in Budget 2026 expenditures and any additional provincial borrowing required to finance the deficit path described in the fiscal plan.122 The Scotiabank analysis of Manitoba's budget notes fiscal balance is contingent on federal transfers and revenue projections being realized in the current rate environment.4

provinces.name: Nova Scotia
provinces.analysis:
Nova Scotia's unemployment rate rose to 7.1% in February 2026, up from 6.9% the prior month, while the employment rate declined to 57.0% from 57.1% and the participation rate fell to 61.3% from 61.4%, according to Statistics Canada.1 CMHC recorded 7,146 annualized housing starts in Nova Scotia for February 2026, down from 7,252 in January, marking a second consecutive monthly decline in new residential construction activity.2 Annual real GDP growth of 2.7% was recorded for 2024, the most recent full-year provincial estimate published by StatCan.1

Hydro-Québec issued a formal request for information from energy developers to assess the feasibility of connecting its provincial electricity grid with Nova Scotia's proposed offshore wind farms, covering development timelines and costs for transmission lines and supporting infrastructure.4 The utility stated its objective is to evaluate timelines and costs before making any project commitment. No dollar values, capacity targets, or development timelines were disclosed in the RFI materials.4

Prime Minister Mark Carney and Premier Tim Houston signed a bilateral agreement in Halifax to coordinate and simplify federal and provincial environmental review processes for major infrastructure and resource projects in Nova Scotia.3 Nova Scotia's 2026-27 Budget, tabled in February 2026, projects a deficit of $1.24 billion, with deficits projected to remain above $1 billion through 2028-29 — a departure from the province's prior deficit reduction trajectory, according to RBC Economics.6 The budget introduces no new personal income taxes but proposes an increase to the financial institutions capital tax effective 2026 and adds a new electric and hybrid vehicle levy effective October 1, 2026.7

Fisheries and Oceans Canada announced management measures for the 2026 elver fishing season covering Southwest Nova Scotia, Cape Breton, and Southwest New Brunswick, citing the economic importance of the elver fishery for commercial licence holders and First Nations communities holding communal commercial licences in the affected regions.5

The federal-provincial environmental review agreement, the Hydro-Québec offshore wind interconnection inquiry, and a provincial budget projecting sustained deficits above $1 billion frame Nova Scotia's near-term capital investment context.346 No individual project announcements, contract awards, or regulatory decisions beyond these developments were reported in this week's provincial news articles.
provinces.sectorHighlights:
The power and energy sector recorded two significant developments this week. Hydro-Québec issued a request for information targeting offshore wind energy developers to assess technical and financial feasibility of a transmission interconnection between Quebec's provincial grid and Nova Scotia's proposed offshore wind installations, covering timelines and costs for transmission infrastructure.4 The federal-provincial environmental review agreement signed by Prime Minister Carney and Premier Houston applies to major energy and resource projects, affecting the approval pathway for offshore wind and other large-scale project development in the province.3 National industry GDP data for utilities and power generation are not available for the current reporting period.

The fisheries sector — a structural component of Nova Scotia's coastal and rural economy — received a federal management framework for the 2026 elver fishing season covering Southwest Nova Scotia and Cape Breton.5 Elver (juvenile American eel) carries significant export value to Asian markets. The 2026 management measures govern both commercial licence holders and First Nations harvesters operating under communal commercial licences in the affected regions.5
provinces.labourDeepDive:
Nova Scotia's participation rate stood at 61.3% in February 2026, down from 61.4% in January, while the employment rate fell to 57.0% from 57.1% over the same period.1 The unemployment rate rose to 7.1% from 6.9%, reflecting a net increase in persons seeking employment relative to the labour force. Housing starts declined to 7,146 annualized units in February from 7,252 in January, indicating moderation in residential construction activity that may affect construction-sector labour demand.2

No sector-specific hiring data, wage trend information, or youth and immigration labour market details were available in this week's provincial news articles. The federal-provincial environmental review agreement announced this week covers major infrastructure and resource projects, but no employment projections or contractor engagements were disclosed in the announcement.3
provinces.consumerPulse: Nova Scotia's CPI stood at +1.5% year-over-year in February 2026, down from +1.7% in January, reflecting a modest easing in consumer price pressures.1 The province's 2026-27 Budget, tabled in February 2026, introduces a new electric and hybrid vehicle levy effective October 1, 2026 and proposes an increase to the financial institutions capital tax — measures that affect vehicle ownership costs and financial services pricing respectively.7 No housing affordability announcements, grocery price data, or retail trend information appeared in this week's Nova Scotia news articles beyond what provincial macroeconomic indicators reflect.
provinces.tradeExposure: Natural gas prices stood at $2.846/MMBtu this week. Nova Scotia's legacy Sable offshore natural gas production has historically supplied Atlantic Canada and northeastern US markets, though volumes from the original Sable Offshore Energy Project have declined materially from peak levels. The province's broader trade profile centres on Halifax's container port, lobster and seafood exports to US and Asian markets, and Irving Shipbuilding's defence contracts under the National Shipbuilding Strategy. Hydro-Québec's feasibility inquiry into connecting Nova Scotia's proposed offshore wind farms to the Quebec provincial grid represents a potential clean electricity export corridor, contingent on RFI results and subsequent project development.4
provinces.marketContext: The Bank of Canada's policy rate stands at 2.25% as of March 2026.8 At this rate level, borrowing costs for capital-intensive projects — including offshore wind transmission infrastructure under Hydro-Québec's feasibility assessment and projects that would advance under the new federal-provincial environmental review framework — reflect conditions below the recent peak rate cycle. Nova Scotia's housing starts fell to 7,146 annualized units in February from 7,252 in January, indicating that residential construction has not re-accelerated materially despite the lower rate environment.2

provinces.analysis:
New Brunswick recorded GDP growth of +1.8% in 2024 according to Statistics Canada data, while the provincial unemployment rate rose to 7.0% in February 2026 from 6.7% the prior month — a 30-basis-point increase.12 The employment rate held at 56.5%, unchanged from the prior period, while the participation rate edged up to 60.7% from 60.6%, indicating that additional residents entered the active labour force during a period of rising unemployment. Housing starts totalled 6,011 units in February 2026, down from 6,454 the prior period.13

The federal government announced nearly $10 million in funding to Saint John Energy to upgrade the city's electricity distribution system under the natural resources ministry's grid modernization program.1 Secretary of State Wayne Long made the announcement on behalf of Energy Minister Tim Hodgson, with the investment targeting improved reliability and sustainability for Saint John's electricity network.2

Finance Minister René Legacy tabled New Brunswick's 2026–2027 budget on March 17, 2026, projecting a $1.33 billion deficit and real GDP growth of 1% for 2026.11 The province attributed the extended deficit to global economic uncertainty and ongoing trade pressures, while directing capital spending toward demographic-driven service gaps.8 Scotiabank's analysis noted the budget signals an extended period of higher deficits across the provincial fiscal plan.10

New Brunswick committed $78 million for construction of two new schools in Dieppe to address enrollment overcrowding driven by population growth in the Greater Moncton area.6 The provincial 2026–2027 budget identified infrastructure investment as a priority in urban centres facing service strain from sustained in-migration.11

Secretary of State Wayne Long also traveled to Fredericton to announce investments under Canada's new Defence Industrial Strategy, targeting local innovation and defence manufacturing in Atlantic Canada, with Member of Parliament David Myles in attendance.3 The Department of Fisheries and Oceans announced federal management measures for the 2026 elver fishing season in Southwest New Brunswick, affirming the fishery as an income source for commercial licence holders and First Nations communities in the region.4
provinces.sectorHighlights:
New Brunswick's power and energy sector recorded a direct federal capital commitment this week: nearly $10 million was allocated to Saint John Energy for electricity distribution system upgrades targeting grid reliability and sustainability in Saint John.1 National industry GDP data for utilities (NAICS 22) is not available for the current period; the investment falls within a federal grid modernization program operating across Atlantic Canada.2 Irving Oil's Saint John refinery — the largest in Canada — operates in the same industrial corridor, making electricity infrastructure a material input for the province's largest processing facility.

New Brunswick's education sector registered the week's largest single capital commitment: $78 million allocated for two new schools in Dieppe in response to population-driven enrollment overcrowding in the Greater Moncton catchment.6 The provincial 2026–2027 budget, tabled March 17, projects a $1.33 billion deficit while directing infrastructure spending toward demographic pressure points concentrated in the province's urban centres.11 National GDP data for education (NAICS 61) is not available for the current period.

The defence sector generated a federal announcement in Fredericton under Canada's new Defence Industrial Strategy, positioning Atlantic Canada — including New Brunswick — as a target region for innovation and defence manufacturing investments.3 Specific project values and recipient organizations from the Fredericton announcement had not been disclosed in available reporting as of March 31, 2026.
provinces.labourDeepDive:
New Brunswick's unemployment rate rose to 7.0% in February 2026 from 6.7% the prior month, a 30-basis-point increase according to Statistics Canada.12 The employment rate held flat at 56.5% — unchanged from the prior period — while the participation rate increased marginally to 60.7% from 60.6%, indicating that more residents entered the labour force during a period when the unemployment rate also rose.

A Fredericton-area restaurant worker profiled by the Globe and Mail, earning $51,000 annually, described chronic health conditions as reducing available work hours and increasing service expenditures — illustrating how health-related constraints affect earnings and spending capacity in the province's service sector.5 Housing starts declined to 6,011 units in February 2026 from 6,454 the prior period, a reduction that moderates residential construction labour demand in the province.13

Population growth in the Greater Moncton area has generated measurable strain on public education infrastructure, with the province committing $78 million for two new schools in Dieppe to reduce overcrowding in existing facilities.6 New Brunswick's CPI registered +1.2% year-over-year in February 2026, down from +2.4% the prior period.12

The federal $10 million investment in Saint John's electricity grid directly supports industrial infrastructure in the same corridor as refinery operations.1 No crude oil throughput or pricing data specific to the Irving facility was reported this week.

provinces.analysis:

The federal Department of Fisheries and Oceans set the 2026 Total Allowable Catch for Newfoundland and Labrador snow crab at 61,004 tonnes, a 3% decrease from the 2025 level, with Minister Joanne Thompson simultaneously announcing the launch of a Precautionary Approach Review for the fishery.1

Premier Tony Wakeham and the Minister of Energy and Mines attended CERAWeek 2026, where the Premier delivered a ministerial statement highlighting efforts to promote Newfoundland and Labrador's energy sector to international investors.4 The Ministry of Forestry, Agriculture and Lands participated in a wildfire preparedness forum hosted by Newfoundland Power on March 31 at Pippy Park, St. John's.5

provinces.name: Prince Edward Island
provinces.analysis:
PEI's GDP grew +3.6% in 2024, according to Statistics Canada data.6 Unemployment fell to 7.2% in February 2026 from 7.6% the prior month — a decline of 0.4 percentage points — while the employment rate rose to 61.8% from 61.5% and the participation rate edged up to 66.6% from 66.5% over the same reference period.6

PEI was identified as one of three provinces — alongside Quebec and British Columbia — to have made meaningful progress on the transition to electric school buses, according to a March 2026 national report card covering Canada's electric school bus transition.3 The report found that cost barriers and provincial policy gaps continue to stall adoption in the majority of Canadian provinces, while PEI's progress was specifically noted among the exceptions.3

The PEI government announced its Capital Budget for 2026-27, outlining a five-year plan that includes the Ministry of Transportation and Economic Corridors' three-year capital plan totaling more than $8.3 billion, subject to legislative approval.4 The PEI Legislature returned on March 24, 2026, and the Canadian Federation of Independent Business issued a pre-budget submission calling on Budget 2026 to keep the provincial small business tax rate at 1%, raise the small business tax threshold, and address fragile small business confidence ahead of the budget tabling.5

The Government of Canada and PEI signed a co-operation agreement implementing a "one project, one review" approach to environmental and impact assessments for major projects, with the stated intent of minimizing duplication between federal and provincial processes.1 The Impact Assessment Agency of Canada described the agreement as part of federal efforts to build a stronger and more resilient economy, enabling both governments to co-ordinate project review timelines for major capital developments in the province.2
provinces.sectorHighlights:
The transportation and infrastructure sector is the largest identified allocation in PEI's Capital Budget 2026-27, with the Ministry of Transportation and Economic Corridors' three-year capital plan totaling more than $8.3 billion.4 National construction sector (NAICS 23) GDP data was not available for this reporting period, limiting cross-reference with the provincial capital plan announcement.

PEI's clean transportation sector was identified as a national leader in a March 2026 report card, ranking PEI alongside Quebec and British Columbia as the only provinces with meaningful progress on the electric school bus transition.3 The report cited cost and policy gaps as barriers for the majority of Canadian provinces, while PEI was cited as an exception.3 National transport and warehousing sector (NAICS 48-49) GDP data was not available for this period.
provinces.labourDeepDive:
PEI's unemployment rate fell to 7.2% in February 2026 from 7.6% the prior month, according to Statistics Canada.6 The employment rate rose simultaneously to 61.8% from 61.5%, and the participation rate increased to 66.6% from 66.5%, indicating concurrent improvement across all three headline labour market indicators in the same reference period.6

No sector-specific hiring or layoff data for PEI was reported in available articles this week. The Canadian Federation of Independent Business's pre-budget submission noted fragile small business confidence in the province as the legislature returned on March 24, 2026, without providing specific sector employment figures.5
provinces.consumerPulse: The Canadian Federation of Independent Business called on PEI's Budget 2026 to keep the provincial small business tax rate at 1% and raise the small business tax threshold, citing fragile small business confidence as the PEI Legislature returned in late March 2026.5 PEI's pre-budget consultation process for the 2026-27 operating budget was open as of March 25, inviting public input on fiscal priorities ahead of the budget tabling.7
provinces.tradeExposure:
PEI accounts for approximately 25% of Canadian potato production, making agriculture the province's primary trade exposure alongside seafood including lobster and mussels.9 No current market price or export volume data for PEI's key agricultural commodities was reported in available articles this week.

As the smallest provincial economy in Canada, PEI's trade dynamics are concentrated in agriculture and seafood exports, with limited diversification into other commodity sectors. The province's tourism sector contributes seasonally to economic activity, with no current tourism volume or revenue data reported for this period.
provinces.marketContext: The Bank of Canada's policy rate stands at 2.25% as of March 2026, setting the borrowing cost baseline for capital projects outlined in PEI's Capital Budget 2026-27.4 PEI's housing starts fell to 963 annualized units in February 2026 from 1,112 the prior month, a decline of approximately 13.4% month-over-month, according to CMHC data.8

provinces.analysis:
Yukon-specific GDP and labour force data are not reported at the territorial level in StatCan's regular monthly releases; the territory's economy is anchored by mining, government services, and federal transfers, with tourism concentrated in summer months around the Klondike region. The Bank of Canada held its policy rate at 2.25% as of March 31, 2026, establishing the borrowing cost environment for Yukon's capital-intensive resource and infrastructure sectors.

Agnico Eagle Mines (NYSE, TSX: AEM) acquired a 14% equity stake in Cascadia Minerals (TSXV: CAM) to support the Carmacks copper-gold project in central Yukon and to advance regional exploration in the territory.2 The two companies announced a strategic alliance focused on identifying and advancing projects within Yukon's Stikine Terrane, a geological corridor extending through the territory's southwest.3

Yukon's energy minister stated the territory's need to upgrade its aging electricity grid has reached a critical level, citing a frigid period that stressed existing power systems.1 Representatives from all three Canadian territories called on the federal government for billions of dollars in infrastructure investment to modernize territorial electricity grids serving small and dispersed populations.1

Yukon's Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources faced legislative questions regarding mining revenues during the week of March 28, 2026.5 The Yukon government separately announced an expansion of family medicine residency training seats and confirmed plans to advance a permanent northern medical training program to address healthcare workforce gaps in the territory.4

The Carmacks copper-gold project received strategic backing through Agnico Eagle's equity acquisition in Cascadia Minerals, connecting a major gold producer to Yukon's exploration pipeline.2 Territorial electricity infrastructure was identified by Yukon and its territorial counterparts as requiring multi-billion-dollar federal commitments to maintain power reliability across remote northern communities.1
provinces.sectorHighlights:
National mining and oil & gas GDP data for this reporting period are not available from StatCan primary sources. Within Yukon, the mining sector recorded a significant equity transaction: Agnico Eagle Mines acquired a 14% stake in Cascadia Minerals (TSXV: CAM), directed at the Carmacks copper-gold project and broader Stikine Terrane exploration.2 Gold traded at $1,445 per troy ounce as of March 31, 2026, the key commodity price context for Yukon's gold-oriented mining activities.3

The energy and utilities sector drew attention as Yukon's energy minister joined counterparts from the Northwest Territories and Nunavut in calling for federal investment in aging territorial electricity infrastructure.1 Territorial representatives characterized the situation as having reached a critical level following a frigid period that tested existing grid capacity, and called on Ottawa for billions in funding to update or sustain territorial power systems.1

The healthcare sector saw a policy development with the Yukon government announcing new family medicine residency training seats and advancing plans for a permanent northern medical training program, with implications for the territorial healthcare workforce.4

The Yukon government's announcement of new family medicine residency training seats signals an expansion of healthcare workforce capacity, with a permanent northern medical training program under development to address workforce gaps in the territory.4 No wage trend or immigration labour dynamic data were reported in available sources for this period.

Energy cost reliability emerged as a consumer-facing concern this week, with territorial energy ministers citing the critical state of aging electricity infrastructure that residents depend on during extreme cold periods.1 The City of Whitehorse issued a public safety advisory about snowmelt hazards following a heavy winter, reflecting seasonal pressures on municipal services and residents.6

Healthcare access remained a public concern, with a letter to the editor raising issues about the Yukon government's health authority decisions, while the government separately announced an expansion of family medicine training capacity.74
provinces.tradeExposure:
Yukon's private-sector economy is driven primarily by mining, with gold, silver, and zinc as key export commodities. Gold traded at $1,445 per troy ounce as of March 31, 2026, providing the commodity price backdrop for projects including the Carmacks copper-gold deposit, which Agnico Eagle and Cascadia Minerals are advancing through a newly formed strategic alliance in the Stikine Terrane.2 Silver stood at $72.68 per troy ounce, relevant to polymetallic deposit economics within the same exploration corridor.3

Federal transfer payments represent a significant component of Yukon's fiscal base alongside resource royalties. Mining revenues came under legislative scrutiny during the reporting week, with Yukon's Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources questioned in the legislature about revenue levels from the resource sector.5
provinces.marketContext:

For the territory, rate conditions primarily affect project financing rather than residential mortgage markets, given Yukon's small population and limited housing market relative to southern provinces.

The multi-billion-dollar electricity grid modernization sought by Yukon and fellow territories from the federal government represents infrastructure financing that is sensitive to long-term borrowing costs, with the current rate environment a factor in federal capital allocation decisions.1

Federal infrastructure announcements in Northwest Territories dominated reporting for the week ending March 31, 2026, with Prime Minister Mark Carney's confirmation of support for the Taltson Hydro expansion marking the territory's highest-profile capital development in available sources.1 Northwest Territories does not report monthly territorial GDP or labour force data on the same cycle as provinces through StatCan primary data series; territorial economic data is published on annual or periodic schedules.

The federal government confirmed backing for the Taltson Hydro expansion following Prime Minister Carney's northern spending announcement during a visit to Yellowknife earlier in March 2026.1 The project is described as ambitious in scope and had limited public profile outside the territory prior to the federal announcement.1 The Taltson Hydro project represents the most significant energy infrastructure development for Northwest Territories reported in available news sources this week.

The Government of Northwest Territories announced it will pursue financing through the federal Arctic Infrastructure Fund to fund construction of a second terminal at Yellowknife Airport.2 Updates to the existing airport terminal are scheduled to commence in summer 2026.2 The Arctic Infrastructure Fund is a federal capital program supporting infrastructure in Canada's northern and remote regions.

The GNWT opened a public consultation period on a draft boreal caribou range plan for the Wek'èezhìı region, releasing a feedback survey for territorial residents and stakeholders.3 Range plans establish habitat boundaries and land-use parameters with regulatory implications for resource extraction projects in the designated area. Stanton Territorial Hospital in Yellowknife implemented a new clinical model under which smoking cessation treatment is incorporated into routine care for patients who smoke.4

The NWT Shelter Network launched a new website consolidating resources for shelter workers and individuals experiencing family violence across the territory.5 Available news sources for the week ending March 31, 2026 did not report additional capital project announcements, budget releases, or fiscal policy changes for Northwest Territories beyond the developments noted above.
provinces.sectorHighlights:
Power and energy infrastructure represented the most active capital sector in Northwest Territories this week. National utility and energy industry GDP data are not available for this reporting period. The federal government's confirmation of support for the Taltson Hydro expansion — described as ambitious and with limited prior national profile — marks a notable development in the territory's power generation portfolio.1 The project was identified as a key component of Prime Minister Carney's northern spending commitment announced in Yellowknife in March 2026.1

Transport infrastructure activity advanced with the GNWT's announcement that it will pursue Arctic Infrastructure Fund financing for a second terminal at Yellowknife Airport, the territory's primary air hub.2 Construction work on updates to the existing terminal is scheduled to begin in summer 2026.2 National construction GDP data for the current reporting period is not available in primary data sources for this report.

Environment and land-use regulation activity continued with the GNWT's public consultation on the Wek'èezhìı boreal caribou range plan.3 Range plan designations carry land-use implications for resource extraction operations in the affected area. No specific company or project was referenced in connection with the consultation in available coverage this week.
provinces.labourDeepDive:
Monthly labour force data for Northwest Territories is not published on the same schedule as provinces under StatCan's Labour Force Survey program. Territorial employment figures for March 2026 are not available in this reporting cycle; StatCan releases territorial labour data periodically through supplementary surveys rather than monthly LFS releases.

The GNWT health sector recorded a service delivery development this week with the implementation of a smoking cessation integration model at Stanton Territorial Hospital in Yellowknife.4 The program incorporates cessation treatment into routine care at the territory's primary acute care facility. No sector-specific hiring announcements, wage data, participation rate changes, or employment trend figures were reported in available news sources for Northwest Territories for the week ending March 31, 2026.
provinces.consumerPulse: Consumer-facing news in Northwest Territories this week centered on social support infrastructure. The NWT Shelter Network launched a new website consolidating resources for shelter workers and individuals affected by family violence across the territory.5 The GNWT integrated smoking cessation treatment into routine clinical care at Stanton Territorial Hospital in Yellowknife.4 No housing affordability developments, energy cost changes, grocery price reporting, or retail sector data were published in available news sources for the territory for the week ending March 31, 2026.
provinces.tradeExposure: Northwest Territories's commodity trade profile centers on diamonds, gold, and zinc. Gold traded at $1,445 this week.6 The territory's diamond mining sector is in a transition phase, with the Diavik and Ekati mines in an operational wind-down phase and remediation projects underway. Indigenous-led resource development represents an emerging category of capital activity in the territory. No commodity shipment data, export volumes, or territorial trade figures were published in available news sources for the week ending March 31, 2026.
provinces.marketContext: The Bank of Canada policy rate stands at 2.25% as of March 31, 2026.6 For capital-intensive infrastructure projects in Northwest Territories — including the Taltson Hydro expansion and the Yellowknife Airport terminal — the current rate level directly affects long-term project financing costs. Federal funding mechanisms such as the Arctic Infrastructure Fund partially offset direct rate exposure for territorial projects, though private capital components remain subject to current borrowing conditions.2

provinces.name: Nunavut
provinces.analysis:
Nunavut-specific GDP, employment, and CPI indicators are not available in primary StatCan data APIs this reporting period. The territory's economy is characterized by federal transfer dominance and resource sector activity, with no provincial statistical release this week.

Federal marine infrastructure was the dominant investment activity. The Government of Canada completed construction of a new small craft harbour in Clyde River, citing Arctic sovereignty, community safety, and fishing economy support as primary rationale.2 Fisheries Minister Joanne Thompson traveled to Iqaluit to announce additional federal investments in small craft harbours across Canada's high Arctic.3

On March 28, the Government of Canada and the Qikiqtani Inuit Association celebrated the formal establishment of the Qikiqtait and Sarvarjuaq Marine Protected Areas in Nunavut, advancing Canada's objective of protecting 30 per cent of the ocean by 2030.1 An Inuit Impact and Benefit Agreement was signed covering both the marine protected areas and terrestrial areas in the Belcher Islands, which are to be designated as Inuit Protected and Conserved Areas.1

In the mining sector, B2Gold (TSX: BTO; NYSE-A: BTG) reported that infill drilling at the Goose area of Nunavut's Back River gold district reinforces the area's expansion potential and the probability of extended mine life at the Back River operation.4 Exploration is described as a cornerstone of B2Gold's strategy at the Back River district.5

A territorial fiscal pressure surfaced as the Canadian insurance market declined to provide coverage for Nunavut hamlets, with the Government of Nunavut's contribution toward insurance coverage increasing to $11.25 million from $850,000.6
provinces.sectorHighlights:
Mining (NAICS 21): National mining and oil and gas extraction GDP data is unavailable this week (M/M N/A, Y/Y N/A). B2Gold reported infill drilling results at the Goose area of the Back River gold district in Nunavut, with results described as reinforcing expansion potential and improving the probability of prolonged mine life at the Back River gold operation.4 B2Gold states exploration remains a core strategic component at the site.5

Marine Infrastructure and Environment: The completion of the federal small craft harbour in Clyde River adds community marine infrastructure supporting Arctic access and sovereignty in Nunavut.2 The establishment of the Qikiqtait and Sarvarjuaq Marine Protected Areas, accompanied by a signed Inuit Impact and Benefit Agreement covering marine and Belcher Islands terrestrial areas, represents a formal expansion of protected ocean territory in the territory.1
provinces.labourDeepDive:
Province-specific labour market indicators for Nunavut — including participation rate, employment rate, and unemployment rate — are not available in primary StatCan data this reporting period. No sector-specific hiring announcements or layoff disclosures appeared in Nunavut-focused articles this week.

B2Gold's ongoing infill drilling program at the Back River gold district reflects continued operational activity in Nunavut's mining sector, which is among the territory's primary private-sector employers, though no employment figures or workforce updates were disclosed in this week's reporting.4
provinces.consumerPulse: The Canadian insurance market's withdrawal from coverage for Nunavut hamlets resulted in the Government of Nunavut's contribution toward insurance costs increasing to $11.25 million from $850,000, transferring a substantially larger fiscal burden to the territorial government for municipal liability coverage.6 No grocery price, housing affordability, or energy cost data specific to Nunavut was reported in this week's articles beyond a criminal incident at an Iqaluit grocery establishment.6
provinces.tradeExposure: Nunavut's primary commodity exposures are gold, iron ore (Baffinland Mary River mine), and diamonds. Gold traded at $1,445 this week. B2Gold's Back River gold mine is the territory's principal gold-producing operation, and this week's infill drilling results at the Goose area indicate active exploration activity within the district.4 The Baffinland Mary River iron ore operation remains the territory's largest single employer; no specific production, shipment, or pricing data for iron ore from the Mary River operation was reported this week. Federal transfers constitute the dominant revenue source for the territorial government, limiting direct commodity price transmission to territorial fiscal accounts.
provinces.marketContext: The Bank of Canada's policy rate stands at 2.25%. For Nunavut, where capital projects are predominantly federally financed and private-sector activity is concentrated in mining, the rate environment affects financing costs for resource extraction operations and any territorial infrastructure debt instruments. Nunavut's housing stock is dominated by social and government housing, reducing direct rate sensitivity relative to southern Canadian markets.
